### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is an absurd one.”

French

“Le doute n'est pas un état bien agréable, mais l'assurance est un état ridicule.”

“Doubt is not a very agreeable state, but assurance is a ridiculous one.” From a letter, not a published work.

### Attribution notes

The line comes from Voltaire's correspondence — a letter of November 1770 — rather than from the Philosophical Dictionary or any of the works usually cited for it. Like most of Voltaire's sharpest sentences it was written to one reader, which is why the phrasing is looser than his published prose.

#### About Voltaire

Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet, 1694–1778) was the French Enlightenment’s sharpest satirist and campaigner for toleration, author of Candide and countless polemics. Imprisoned in the Bastille, exiled in England, resident at Cirey and Ferney, he fought judicial fanaticism in cases such as Calas.

### How to read this passage

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, wisdom.
